origin_region: Hsinchu and Miaoli (Oriental Beauty), Nantou (Gui Fei oolong, honey black tea), Hualien; the idea is now copied in Fujian, Guangdong and Japan
cultivar: Qing Xin Da Mou for classic Oriental Beauty; Qing Xin, Jin Xuan and others for Gui Fei and bug-bitten black and white teas
processing: Not a factory step but a field condition: the tea green leafhopper (Jacobiasca formosana) feeds on young shoots in summer, and the plant responds by producing defensive compounds that turn into honey, muscat and ripe-fruit aromas once the leaf is oxidised. The bitten leaf is picked small and made into a heavily oxidised, unroasted oolong (Oriental Beauty), a ball-rolled roasted oolong (Gui Fei), or a black or white tea. It requires an unsprayed garden, since any insecticide kills the leafhoppers.
harvest_season: Summer, June to July, when the leafhopper population peaks in warm, humid weather; the hottest, buggiest weeks give the strongest honey aroma. A lesser autumn picking exists.
appearance_dry: Small, mottled leaves in several colours, white tips, red, brown, yellow and green together ('five colours') for Oriental Beauty; dark rolled pellets for Gui Fei; the bitten leaves are small, curled and ragged at the edges.
appearance_liquor: Honey-amber to orange-red, bright and clear.
appearance_wet: Small, soft, bronze-and-green leaves with chewed edges and bite marks visible as tiny yellowed spots.
taste_profile: Honey, muscat grape, ripe peach and a touch of cinnamon with a soft, round body and almost no astringency; the honey note is the leafhopper's signature and is strongest in the summer picking.

brewing.notes: Water at 85–90 °C, not boiling, which cooks the honey into caramel; short steeps in a gaiwan or porcelain pot. Western style, 3 g per 250 ml for 3 minutes. It also cold-brews beautifully and is one of the few oolongs that takes a drop of honey without seeming odd.

vintage_note: Sold by the current summer's harvest, in small packs, at prices that reflect the small leaf, the low yields of an unsprayed garden and the labour of picking; competition-grade Oriental Beauty with a high proportion of white tips sells for many times the price of an ordinary lot. The name 'Oriental Beauty' is applied loosely to any heavily oxidised Taiwanese oolong and the honey character is the proof, so taste before paying. Bug-bitten teas keep for years and some Oriental Beauty is sold aged with the year stated.
description:
Bug-bitten tea is the one case in which an insect improves a crop. In Taiwan's hot, humid summers a tiny green leafhopper feeds on the young tea shoots, and the plant fights back with aromatic compounds that, once the leaf is oxidised, taste of honey, muscat grapes and ripe peaches. Oriental Beauty, the heavily oxidised, tippy oolong of Hsinchu and Miaoli, is the famous result; Gui Fei oolong, honey-scented black teas and even some white teas use the same trick.

The craft is mostly in the field. The garden cannot be sprayed, or the leafhoppers die; the shoots are picked small and mottled in the hottest weeks of early summer, when the bugs are busiest, and yields are tiny. The tea is then made with a long wither and a high oxidation, around 60–80 %, and no roast, so that the honey aroma survives; Gui Fei takes the same bitten leaf through ball-rolling and a light roast for a darker, caramelised version.

The cup is amber and soft, honeyed and fruity with cinnamon at the edges and no bite, and it is nearly impossible to brew badly as long as the water is not boiling, which turns the honey to burnt sugar. Water around 85 °C, short steeps, several infusions; cold brew it and it tastes like white grape juice.

It is a summer tea sold in the current year, and it is expensive because of how little a bug-bitten garden yields; the signal of a real one is the honey note itself, since the name gets stuck on ordinary dark oolongs. Competition grades with many white tips cost a great deal; an honest mid-grade lot from a named farm is the sensible buy, and it keeps for years.

The Taiwan group's Oriental Beauty card covers the specific tea; this card is the phenomenon. To taste it, compare a bug-bitten summer lot with a spring tea from the same farm and cultivar: the honey is only in one of them.
